items.reason: Pinning a tag to a digest requires asking GitHub what the tag points at right now, and this session has no network; the repository already records exactly this in .github/contract-ledger.json (rule `P4 action-sha-pin`), whose verdict says closing it is one networked `npm run actions:pin`. The broad-write half needs no change: .github/workflow-permissions.json already declares all seven write grants, and the only `contents: write` (issue-dispatch.yml#push) is documented as split from the jobs holding the model key and the PR scope.

Diagnosed but not closable here. Rule A5 does catch every narrating subject in the recent sample (I checked them against scripts/commit-subject.mjs), so the rule is right; what fails is reach — the commits that carry them are written by lanes in throwaway worktrees, and the two hooks that would refuse them at write time (.husky/commit-msg, .husky/prepare-commit-msg) are GENERATED by `npm install` rather than tracked, so a worktree that never ran it has none. Committing those two files byte-identically to HOOKS in scripts/install-commit-hooks.mjs closes it; this session's permission layer refused every write under .husky/. Separately: scripts/agent-review.mjs:129 exits before A5 whenever the net diff is empty, so a commit range with no net change is never subject-checked.

The declaration already exists and is thorough (.github/agent-permissions.json: 7 rules, 21 deny / 9 ask / 22 allow, each quoted from AGENTS.md with what the pattern cannot see). What is missing is only the ENFORCED half: .claude/settings.json carries no permissions block, so `npm run agent:permissions:check` is red today. I wrote out the exact block and both Write and Edit were refused by this session's permission layer for that path. One command closes it: `npm run agent:permissions -- --install`, then commit the file.

Added docs/security/threat-model.md: every credential (operator-wide and per-tenant) with where it enters, where it rests, where it leaves, which contexts may see it and which fence stands on it; which of the eslint.config.mjs seams are security vs architecture; the read-order for the BYOM key path; and what the model cannot see. Routed from docs/task-index.md and SECURITY.md, and given an age budget in .github/docs-staleness.json watching the seams it names.

Added .github/workflows/post-deploy.yml + scripts/post-deploy-verify.mjs: on every push to master (the release act) it polls /api/health — the readiness probe that already existed and that nothing was wired to — for up to five minutes and fails the run when the release does not report ok, when Firestore is unreadable with credentials present, or on a 401 (which is also a cron outage). Verdict kept as a 90-day artifact with the runbook's next command. Deliberately does NOT auto-revert: that needs a token that can write refs/heads/master, which AGENTS.md § Red forbids. Absence of CRON_SECRET/ADAMANT_HEALTH_URL records `status: "skipped"` rather than a green, declared as the `post-deploy-verify` capability so harness:degradation:check holds it.

Added a held-out tier no --reason can reach: test-llm/held-out.mjs pins three prompt invariants whose absence changes what the product tells an advertiser (no invented figures across 14 grounded tools, no external benchmarks in the three client-facing reporting tools, efficiency-is-not-profitability in analysis+chat). scripts/llm-eval.mjs --update now checks them BEFORE writing a byte and refuses; test-unit/golden-held-out.test.mjs runs the same check against the committed goldens on every build (so a hand-edited golden, which passes the drift check by construction, is caught) and proves the check still detects by gutting a golden fixture.

Already covered another way, in both halves. Scoping the expensive half exists: `npm run test:fast` + .github/test-tiers.json select the suites that NAME a changed file, derived from the tests' own text so the mapping cannot rot, deliberately never a gate — which is the exact answer to 'how would a fast subset avoid becoming the real gate'. Declaring the seam each gate defends exists too: .github/constraint-map.json is keyed by rule and names its gate, and test-unit/constraint-map.test.mjs turns the suite red when a check:ci stage has no rule attached. What remains is not scopable: eleven of the fourteen cheap gates are cross-reference checkers (adr:check verifies cited paths anywhere, agents:surface counts unmapped source files, contract:ledger measures counts across the tree), so a docs-only change can genuinely break most of them — which .github/test-tiers.json's `always` tier already states in prose. I added my two new census tests to that tier rather than inventing a second selector.

Added test-unit/contract.mjs: a failure message builder that cites the broken rule out of .github/constraint-map.json (id, sentence, rung, the fences enforcing it, where it is stated, and the route to the record that decided it) and throws on an id the map does not carry. Applied to the two money/breach seam suites the mutation catalogue names that have a rule id — cron-auth (security-rules) and campaigns-mutator (no-live-ad-writes). test-unit/failure-contract.test.mjs blocks: every cited id must exist in the map, every mutation-catalogue seam suite must cite a rule or be on a ceilinged exception list with its reason, every path in a rendered message must exist, and an unknown id must still be refused.

lessons: In this repository every fence is a two-part diff: the thing you add, and the declaration that pays for it. A doc costs a docs-staleness entry and a task-index route; a task-index route costs a line in .github/guidance-budget.json; a workflow costs a .github/workflow-permissions.json entry; a key-gated step costs a capability in scripts/harness-degradation.mjs. Landing only the first half is what turns the build red, and finding the second half is most of the work.

Before writing a new gate here, check whether the reporting-plus-ratchet version already exists under a different name — test:fast/.github/test-tiers.json, the constraint map, the contract ledger and gate-remedy already cover a lot of ground that reads as missing from outside.

A sandboxed lane can be blocked from the exact file that closes an item: .claude/settings.json and .husky/* were unwritable here, which turned two otherwise one-command items into handoffs. Worth checking write access to the target path before planning the work.

The commit subject an outer lane writes is the agent's report's first line. On a repo with a blocking subject rule, the report's first line has to be written as a conventional-commit subject or the lane's own commit is the one that violates the rule it just helped enforce.
